```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mzLibR)
# Every call on this page is answered from a recording of the real bridge, made on the small
# databases in pyMzLib's test fixtures, so the page builds anywhere. With a bridge installed, the
# same calls read your databases.
.mzlibr_example <- mzLibR:::replay_bridge_start()
```

A search result names proteins by accession. The questions it cannot answer on its own are
answered by mzLib from the protein database you searched:

| question | function | mzLib |
|---|---|---|
| what is this accession: organism, taxon, genes, GO terms? | `proteins_read()` | `ProteinDbLoader` |
| which Ensembl gene is it, reproducibly? | `proteins_resolve_genes()` | `EnsemblGeneResolver` |
| does this peptide identify one protein? | `proteins_classify_peptides()` | `PeptideUniquenessClassifier` |
| which GO terms does each protein group carry, every member kept? | `proteins_annotate_go()` | `GoGroupAnnotator` (#1353), `ToGoAnnotationGroups` (#1366) |
| where do I get a go.obo, and keep it pinned? | `proteins_update_go()` | `Loaders.UpdateGeneOntology` (#1353) |
| where is residue 120 of this protein in its isoform, or in the bovine protein? | `proteins_align()`, `proteins_map_source_to_target()` | `PairwiseAligner` (#1428) |
| which entry, isoform and variants does `P04637-2_S70N` or `NP_000537.3_R72P` name? | `proteins_parse_accessions()` | `VariantApplication.ParseAccession` (#1382) |
| which mouse genes are orthologous to this human gene, and if none, why not? | `proteins_build_orthology()` | `OrthologySnapshot`, `OrthologySnapshotWriter` (#1381) |

The first three take one database or several - UniProt XML or FASTA, optionally gzipped - and
read several in **one** bridge call, `threads` at a time. Mark contaminant databases with
`contaminants`: it changes answers.

## What is this accession?

```{r}
db <- proteins_read(c("human_subset.xml", "human_extra.fasta", "mouse_aifm1.fasta"),
                    contaminants = "contaminants.fasta",
                    tables = c("proteins", "go_terms", "ensembl_genes"))
db
db$proteins[, c("accession", "organism", "ncbi_taxonomy_id", "primary_gene_name",
                "length", "monoisotopic_mass", "is_contaminant")]
```

`length` is in residues and `monoisotopic_mass` in daltons, of the unmodified sequence as written
plus one water - the precursor, not the mature protein. `ncbi_taxonomy_id` is kept a string: it
is an identifier, not a quantity.

GO terms and Ensembl gene links are long tables, one row per protein and term or transcript,
returned only when asked for:

```{r}
head(db$go_terms[, c("accession", "go_id", "aspect", "term_name")])
db$ensembl_genes[, c("accession", "gene_id", "versioned_gene_id", "gene_version")]
```

### A FASTA cannot say

A FASTA header carries organism, taxon and gene name, and nothing else. So a FASTA contributes no
GO or Ensembl rows - and says so, rather than leaving the tables silently short:

```{r}
db$files[, c("file_type", "contaminant", "protein_count")]
db$files$absent_fields
```

Empty there means "this format is silent", never "this protein has none". Read the UniProt XML
of the same proteome for those.

`source_index` in every table is 1-based, so it indexes `files` directly:

```{r}
table(basename(db$files$path[db$proteins$source_index]))
```

To look up only some accessions, pass them as `accessions`. The match is **exact**, so an isoform
suffix that the database does not use is reported, not guessed at:

```{r}
found <- proteins_read(c("human_subset.xml", "human_extra.fasta", "mouse_aifm1.fasta"),
                       contaminants = "contaminants.fasta",
                       accessions = c("P04406", "Q9Z0X1", "P02769", "P04406-1"))
setNames(found$proteins$ncbi_taxonomy_id, found$proteins$accession)
found$accessions_not_found
```

## Which gene is it, reproducibly?

`proteins_resolve_genes()` resolves each protein to stable Ensembl gene ids, **counted against a
gene set you supply**: an Ensembl GTF for one release. Nothing is downloaded or defaulted, because
the release is part of the answer.

```{r}
genes <- proteins_resolve_genes(c("human_subset.xml", "human_extra.fasta"),
                                contaminants = "contaminants.fasta",
                                gtf = "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.gtf",
                                xref = "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.uniprot.tsv")
genes$gene_set[c("source_file_name", "release", "genome_build")]
genes$outcome_counts
genes$resolutions[, c("accession", "outcome", "n_genes", "gene_id", "gene_symbol",
                      "off_primary_genes", "ensembl_xref_agrees")]
```

Every protein gets exactly one outcome. A `multi_gene` protein has one row per gene, never a
pick. `off_primary_only` means its genes exist only on ALT haplotypes or patches outside the gene
set - use Ensembl's primary-assembly GTF. `ensembl_xref_agrees` is `NA` when there is nothing to
compare, which is unknown, not false. Keep `genes$gene_set$sha256` with your results: it pins the
exact gene set.

## Does this peptide identify one protein?

```{r}
calls <- proteins_classify_peptides(
  c("VGVNGFGR", "LVLNGNPLTLFQER", "ALSEQINIFFDYSGR", "YLYEIAR", "AEFVEVTK", "PEPTIDEK"),
  c("human_subset.xml", "human_extra.fasta"),
  contaminants = "contaminants.fasta")
calls$peptides[, c("peptide", "sharing", "accession_count")]
calls$sharing_counts
```

- `LVLNGNPLTLFQER` is GAPDH's `LVINGNPITIFQER`: **I and L are one residue**, because a mass
  spectrometer cannot tell them apart.
- `ALSEQINIFFDYSGR` is in three isoforms of one gene: `SharedWithinGene` supports the gene, not
  an isoform.
- `YLYEIAR` is in human and bovine albumin, which share no gene. Leave the contaminant database
  out and it would read as `Unique`.

```{r}
calls$peptides$accessions[[4]]
calls$peptides$shared_gene_keys[[3]]
```

Containment, not digestion: a protein contains a peptide if its sequence contains it anywhere,
whatever the protease. That is deliberately conservative, so a peptide called `Unique` cannot be
explained by another entry at a site the search's cleavage rules skipped.

## Which GO terms does each protein group carry?

A search reports *protein groups*, and a group can have several members: two histone H2A.Z
variants no peptide could tell apart are one group, `P0C0S5|Q71UI9`. Taking the first accession
throws away half the evidence, and it is not even a choice MetaMorpheus made: it sorts members and
never picks a leading protein. And UniProt records the most specific terms, so a protein annotated
to *mitochondrial inner membrane* is not, as written, "in the mitochondrion" at all.

`proteins_annotate_go()` answers both, with mzLib's `GoGroupAnnotator` reading the protein-group
table MetaMorpheus wrote: **one row per (group, term)** that *any* member holds, directly or
through an ancestor (`is_a` and `part_of`), and every row says which members carry it. The data
here is real: mzLib's copy of a MetaMorpheus 1.1.11 protein-group table from PXD036557, the
UniProt entries it names, and GO release 2026-07-26, trimmed to the terms those proteins reach.

### First, get a go.obo - once, and keep it

Terms are added, renamed and moved between GO releases, so a GO result means something only
relative to one release. `proteins_annotate_go()` never downloads anything; fetching is its own
function, called on purpose:

```{r}
update <- proteins_update_go("go.obo")
update$go[c("release", "term_count")]
```

Call it again later and a newer release replaces the file, while the old one is kept beside it
as `go.obo.<timestamp>`, so a result you already published can still be reproduced.

### Annotate the groups

```{r}
go <- proteins_annotate_go("PXD036557_AllQuantifiedProteinGroups.tsv", "pxd036557_proteins.xml",
                           go_obo = "go-pxd036557.obo", category_map = "organelle_map.tsv")
go
c(table_rows = go$table_row_count, decoys = go$decoy_group_count, groups = go$group_count,
  rows = go$row_count)
```

The decoy group is skipped, because decoys carry no GO. Albumin, a contaminant, gets one row with
no term, and its `annotation_status` says why:

```{r}
go$annotations[go$annotations$protein_group == "P02769",
               c("protein_group", "go_id", "annotation_status", "n_with", "n_members")]
```

Both histones are annotated to the nucleosome, each on its own evidence:

```{r}
histones <- go$annotations[go$annotations$protein_group == "P0C0S5|Q71UI9", ]
nucleosome <- histones[histones$go_id %in% "GO:0000786", ]
nucleosome[, c("go_name", "aspect", "n_with", "n_members", "propagated", "inherited")]
nucleosome$accession_used[[1]]
nucleosome$evidence_by_member[[1]]
```

### Union, consensus, direct only: filters, not modes

The table is the **union** over a group's members. Everything narrower is one comparison on the
rows:

```{r}
c(union = nrow(histones), consensus = sum(histones$n_with == histones$n_members),
  direct = sum(!histones$propagated))
histones$accession_used[histones$go_name %in% "euchromatin"]
```

*Euchromatin* is one histone's term, not the other's. For an enrichment tool that propagates on
its own, keep the rows with `propagated` false.

### In your own vocabulary

`category_map` maps terms to the categories you care about, through anchors: a term belongs to a
category when the anchor is the term or one of its ancestors. mzLib ships no vocabulary.

```{r}
head(go$categories$records)
```

### Pin what you used

Keep `go$go$sha256` and `go$annotation_database$sha256` with your results. The header's counters
count **groups at q <= 0.01**, not rows; the rows themselves are never filtered on q.

```{r}
go$go[c("release", "sha256")]
go$header[c("counter_q_value_max", "status_annotated", "status_contaminant")]
```

When the UniProt XML is newer than the go.obo it cites terms the release lacks, and the call fails
naming every one. Fetch a newer go.obo, or pass `skip_unknown_go_ids = TRUE` to drop those ids and
have them listed in `unresolved_go_ids`.

## Map a residue from one sequence onto another

A position means something only in the sequence it was counted in. A phosphosite reported on the
canonical isoform, a variant called against last year's UniProt release, a cysteine you know in the
human protein: before you look for it in an isoform, an ortholog or a newer entry, you need the
residue that *corresponds* to it there. Counting the same number along the other sequence is wrong
as soon as there is one insertion or deletion before it.

`proteins_align()` aligns pairs of sequences with mzLib's `PairwiseAligner` (#1428) and maps every
residue to its counterpart in the other sequence, or to `NA` when it has none. Here the canonical
DYNC1I2 sequence (Q13409) is aligned with its isoforms 2B and 2C, read from the database with
`sequences = TRUE`:

```{r}
seqs <- proteins_read("human_extra.fasta", contaminants = "contaminants.fasta",
                      accessions = c("Q13409", "Q13409-2", "Q13409-3", "P02768", "P02769"),
                      sequences = TRUE)
seq <- setNames(seqs$proteins$sequence, seqs$proteins$accession)
isoforms <- proteins_align(list(c(seq[["Q13409"]], seq[["Q13409-2"]]),
                                c(seq[["Q13409"]], seq[["Q13409-3"]])))
two <- proteins_alignments(isoforms)
p <- c(75, 76, 82, 100, 120, 133)
data.frame(canonical = p,
           isoform_2B = proteins_map_source_to_target(two[[1]], p),
           isoform_2C = proteins_map_source_to_target(two[[2]], p))
```

Reading it row by row:

- **Up to residue 75 the numbers agree.** Both isoforms begin with the same 75 residues.
- **Residues 76 to 81 have no counterpart in either isoform**: `NA`, never the nearest residue.
- **After the gap the numbers are shifted**: canonical residue 100 is residue 94 of each isoform.
- **Isoform 2C lacks 20 more** (canonical 113 to 132), so canonical 120 has no counterpart in 2C,
  and canonical 133 is 2C's residue 107.

`proteins_map_target_to_source()` goes the other way. The aligned rows hold `-` wherever a residue
faces a gap, so printing them one above the other shows where the gaps fall:

```{r}
writeLines(substr(c(isoforms$records$aligned_source[[2]], isoforms$records$aligned_target[[2]]), 61, 140))
isoforms$records[, c("pair_index", "identical", "substituted", "source_residues_facing_gap")]
isoforms$aligner_id
```

`identical` and `substituted` count the paired residues that are the same letter and that differ;
`source_residues_facing_gap` and `target_residues_facing_gap` count the residues with no
counterpart. `score` is the alignment's BLOSUM62 score in half-bits (see the traps). `aligner_id`
names the method and every parameter, so store it beside any position you map.

### Orthologs: the counterpart can be a different amino acid

Across species most residues still pair, but many pair with a *different* residue. Human serum
albumin's free thiol, Cys34 of the mature protein, is residue 58 of the UniProt sequence, which
counts the 24-residue signal peptide and propeptide. In bovine albumin it is a cysteine at 58 too:

```{r}
albumin <- proteins_align(list(c(seq[["P02768"]], seq[["P02769"]])))
albumin$records[, c("identical", "substituted", "source_residues_facing_gap")]
map <- albumin$residue_map
map[map$sequence == "source" & map$position %in% c(26, 58),
    c("position", "residue", "mapped_position", "mapped_residue")]
```

Residue 26 pairs, but it is A in human and T in bovine albumin. **Always check the residue at the
mapped position** before you carry a modification across: a phosphosite on S is not a site on A.
The residue map puts both letters side by side.

### The options, and whose defaults they are

Every option you leave out is **mzLib's to set**. mzLibR sends nothing for it, and the result says
what the aligner used. The isoform alignment above passed no options, so these are mzLib's own
defaults in this build:

```{r}
str(unclass(isoforms)[c("matrix", "gap_open", "gap_extend", "end_gaps", "max_cells")])
```

| argument | meaning |
|---|---|
| `gap_open` | cost of opening a gap, in BLOSUM62's half-bits; a gap of *k* residues costs `gap_open + k * gap_extend` (BLAST's convention; mzLib's defaults are BLASTP's) |
| `gap_extend` | cost of each residue in a gap, the first included |
| `end_gaps` | `"free"`: an overhang at either end costs nothing (EMBOSS needle's default), so a signal peptide or a longer tail is not penalised. `"charged"`: every gap costs |
| `max_cells` | the largest table mzLib will build, `(nchar(source) + 1) * (nchar(target) + 1)` cells of one byte; a larger pair is refused rather than allowed to exhaust memory |
| `residue_map` | `FALSE` leaves out the residue map, for a large batch where you want only the scores and counts |

```{r}
charged <- proteins_align(list(c("MLLLPEPTIDE", "PEPTIDE")), end_gaps = "charged")
charged$records[, c("aligned_target", "score")]
charged$aligner_id
```

With free end gaps the same pair scores 39: the four-residue overhang costs `11 + 4 * 1` only
when it is charged.

### The traps

- **`score` is not an identity, a bit score or an E-value.** It is a raw sum of BLOSUM62 scores in
  half-bits, less the gaps, and it grows with length. Compare scores only between alignments with
  the same `aligner_id`. mzLibR computes no percent identity, because there are several
  definitions: divide `identical` by the length you mean.
- **It is a global alignment.** Every residue of both sequences is placed, paired or facing a gap.
  With free end gaps a short sequence is placed on the best-scoring stretch of a long one, even
  when it has no real match there.
- **One optimal alignment, chosen the same way every time.** Isoform 2B above is a real case:
  canonical V76 and V82 are both V, either could pair with the isoform's V76, and mzLib pairs V82.
  Another aligner may give the equally good other answer.
- **Pass bare one-letter sequences.** mzLib refuses only `-` and `.`, as an `mzlib_usage_error`.
  Any other character BLOSUM62 does not name - selenocysteine `U`, pyrrolysine `O`, a digit, a
  space, a modification bracket - is scored as an unknown residue `X`, silently.
- **Long pairs need a larger `max_cells`.** Two titin isoforms need about 1.2 billion cells, past
  the default; mzLib accepts up to 2,147,483,591.
- **Many pairs are one call.** `proteins_align()` takes the whole list at once, in one bridge
  process, so a few thousand pairs cost one start-up; never loop it.

## Read an accession into entry, isoform and variants

The accessions a search reports are not all plain entries. UniProt isoforms carry `-2`; RefSeq
accessions carry a `.3` version; and mzLib names a protein with applied sequence variants after
its entry, `P04637_S70N_A80T` or `NP_000537.3_R72P`. To join results to anything you keep per
entry - genes, orthologs, GO terms - you need the entry back, without losing the isoform or the
variants. Cutting at the first `_` turns `NP_000537` into `NP`.

`proteins_parse_accessions()` reads each accession with mzLib's own grammars
(`VariantApplication.ParseAccession`, #1382):

```{r}
parsed <- proteins_parse_accessions(c("P04637", "P04637-2", "Q13409-2", "NP_000537.3_R72P",
  "P04637_S70N_A80T", "P04637_2", "DECOY_P02768", "sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN", "P04637|P02768"))
parsed$records[, c("input", "namespace", "entry_accession", "isoform", "version", "applied_variants")]
parsed$namespace_counts
```

- **`entry_accession`** is the UniProt entry or the unversioned RefSeq accession. It answers "same
  entry?", **not** "same sequence?": `P04637` and `P04637-2` share it, but they are different
  sequences. Join per-entry data on it; join sequence-level data on `input`.
- **`isoform`** and **`version`** are the `-n` and `.n` numbers, `NA` when there is none.
- **`parent_accession`** is the entry the variants were applied to, isoform or version kept:
  `NP_000537.3` for `NP_000537.3_R72P`. Look the parent sequence up under it.
- **`applied_variants`** is the variant suffix exactly as written, `NA` when there is none. It is
  not checked against any sequence.
- **`namespace`** is `uniprot`, `refseq` or `unrecognized`, spelled as `proteins_resolve_genes()`
  spells it, so the two tables join.

**It parses and never repairs.** Everything outside the two grammars comes back `unrecognized`,
with `entry_accession` equal to the input, so a data problem stays visible instead of being fixed
silently. **`P04637_2` is not a variant of P04637**: it is mzLib's loader counter for a
*different* entry whose accession collided with P04637's. Decoy, contaminant and entrapment
prefixes and FASTA headers are left as they are. A protein group (`P04637|P02768`) is not split:
split groups on `|` first, if that is what you mean. Lower case and spaces count, because mzLibR
sends every accession exactly as you give it. Only RefSeq *protein* accessions (`NP_`, `XP_`,
`YP_`, `WP_`, `AP_`) are recognized, so a transcript (`NM_`) or an Ensembl id is unrecognized too.

## Orthologs across species: an Ensembl Compara snapshot

You have a mouse result and a human question: which human gene is this mouse gene's ortholog?
Ensembl Compara answers that, per species pair, in bulk files with three traps:

1. **The dumps partition.** Each species has its own homology dump, and Compara puts each of a
   pair's relationships in *one* of the pair's two dumps, arbitrarily. In release 116 every
   human-mouse orthology is in the **mouse** dump and none is in the human one. Reading the dump
   named after your species gives a complete-looking, badly incomplete answer.
2. **Orthology is not transitive.** Human A ~ mouse B and mouse B ~ rat C does not make A ~ C.
   Chaining pairs into groups invents tuples Compara never asserted.
3. **"No ortholog" means three things.** The gene's tree may hold a gene of the other species with
   no ortholog called, hold none of that species, or the gene may be in no tree at all.

`proteins_build_orthology()` builds mzLib's orthology snapshot (`OrthologySnapshot`, #1381), which
makes the first trap structural - **mzLib refuses a call without every species' dump** - and keeps
the other two visible. This example is mzLib's own test world: four human genes, three mouse and
two rat, with every human-mouse row in the mouse dump. The species are named by Ensembl
production name, the names of `gtfs`:

```{r}
gtfs <- c(homo_sapiens = "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.gtf",
          mus_musculus = "Mus_musculus.GRCm39.116.gtf",
          rattus_norvegicus = "Rattus_norvegicus.GRCr8.116.gtf")
dumps <- paste0("homologies/", names(gtfs), "/Compara.116.protein_default.homologies.tsv.gz")
snap <- proteins_build_orthology("116", gtfs = gtfs, dumps = dumps,
  gene_trees = "vertebrates.GeneTree_content.default.e116.txt.gz",
  pair_status = c("homo_sapiens", "mus_musculus"))   # every human gene, in mouse
snap$pair_status$records[, c("gene_id", "gene_biotype", "status")]
substr(snap$snapshot_id, 1, 12)
```

Record `snap$snapshot_id` with any result you draw from the snapshot. It is mzLib's sha256 over
the format, the release, the species and every input's sha256, so the same inputs always give the
same id, and a different id means different inputs.

### Every species' dump, always

The result shows where the rows came from. The human dump holds one row (human-rat); all three
human-mouse rows came from the mouse dump:

```{r}
snap$dumps[, c("species", "rows_read", "rows_kept")]
snap$pairs
proteins_orthology_pair(snap, "mus_musculus", "homo_sapiens")$row_count   # either order
```

Leave the mouse dump out and mzLib refuses: *"No homology dump for mus_musculus. Each pair's
relationships are split between its two species' dumps, so every species' dump is required."*
That is an `mzlib_usage_error`. A pair with nothing in it, such as the human paralogs here, still
has its row.

### What to download, once per release

Nothing is downloaded for you. For release 116, from `https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-116/`:

| input | path under the release | size (human, 116) | argument |
|---|---|---|---|
| each species' primary-assembly GTF | `gtf/homo_sapiens/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.gtf.gz` | 141 MB | `gtfs = c(species = path)` |
| each species' homology dump | `tsv/ensembl-compara/homologies/homo_sapiens/Compara.116.protein_default.homologies.tsv.gz` | 109 MB | `dumps` |
| the gene trees, one file for all species | `compara/vertebrates.GeneTree_content.default.e116.txt.gz` | 79 MB | `gene_trees` |

**Take the dump in each species' own folder**: every species' dump has the same file name, and
one folder up, `homologies/` also holds a 10 GB file of that name, which is not one species' dump.
**Keep Ensembl's file names**: mzLib holds the gene trees and every dump to `release` only when
their names carry it, and a caveat says which were not checked. A compact gene table made with
mzLib's `EnsemblGeneSetWriter` for `proteins_resolve_genes()` works too, in `gene_sets` instead of
`gtfs`; it carries the GTF's provenance, so the snapshot and its id are the same.

### What each status means

`pair_status = c(from, to)` gives every gene of `from`'s gene set exactly one status in `to`. It
says how far Compara's inference got, not what biology holds:

| status | what it means | read it as |
|---|---|---|
| `has_ortholog` | at least one ortholog in `to` | an answer; the Parquet has the rows |
| `no_edge_in_shared_tree` | the gene's tree holds a `to` gene, and Compara called no ortholog to it | the nearest the data comes to "no ortholog exists" |
| `tree_lacks_target_species` | the gene's tree holds no `to` gene | nothing was compared |
| `not_in_any_tree` | the gene is in the gene set but in no gene tree | no call was attempted |

`snap$pair_status$status_counts` counts genes per status, every status present. **A status is not
symmetric**: ask for `c("mus_musculus", "homo_sapiens")` separately. **Every biotype is a row**, so
choose your denominator by filtering on `gene_biotype`.

### Write the snapshot, then query it

The relationships themselves go to disk. Give `out` a directory that does not exist yet:

```{r}
written <- proteins_build_orthology("116", gtfs = gtfs, dumps = dumps,
  gene_trees = "vertebrates.GeneTree_content.default.e116.txt.gz",
  restrict_gene_trees = TRUE, out = "compara-116")
identical(written$snapshot_id, snap$snapshot_id)
written$written$files[, c("path", "rows", "bytes")]
```

The directory holds `genes/SPECIES.parquet` (the gene set), `members/SPECIES.parquet` (gene to
Compara tree), `pairs/A__B.parquet` (every relationship between A and B, A sorting first; A == B
holds the paralogs), `views.sql` and `manifest.json` (every input and file with its sha256).
**A directory that is not empty is refused**: a snapshot is written once, and next release's goes
in a new directory to compare with this one. `restrict_gene_trees = TRUE` keeps only your
species' genes from the gene-tree file; without it, mzLib's default keeps every gene in it - 4.2
million for the vertebrates of release 116 - and a caveat says how many. The snapshot is the same
either way, as the equal ids show.

**mzLib writes Parquet and ships no reader, and mzLibR reads none** (it has no dependencies). The
`arrow` package reads the tables, and `duckdb` runs the macros mzLib writes in `views.sql`
(`orthologs`, `pair_status`, `species_set3`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not run: needs the arrow package, which mzLibR does not depend on.
pairs <- arrow::read_parquet("compara-116/pairs/homo_sapiens__mus_musculus.parquet")
pairs[pairs$relationship_class == "ortholog",
      c("gene_a", "gene_b", "relationship_type", "identity_a", "identity_b")]
```

`pairs/A__B.parquet` has one row per relationship, ordered by Compara's `homology_id`, with
Compara's values verbatim: `relationship_type` (`ortholog_one2one`, `ortholog_one2many`, ...),
`relationship_class`, the genes and proteins of each side, `identity_a` and `identity_b` (percent,
each over its **own** protein, so they differ), `goc_score`, `wga_coverage`, `dn`, `ds`,
`is_high_confidence` and `source_dump`. **A NULL stays null, never 0 or false**, and arrow reads it
as `NA`. `?proteins_build_orthology` lists every column of the three tables.

### The traps

- **Never chain pairs.** Use `views.sql`'s `species_set3` (or mzLib's `OrthologySnapshot.SpeciesSet`
  for more species), which requires every two members of a tuple to be orthologs.
- **One-to-many is several rows.** Nothing is picked: a human gene with two mouse orthologs has two
  rows, both `ortholog_one2many`. Decide per question.
- **The gene set and the dumps must be one release.** A homology naming a gene its gene set lacks
  is refused as an `mzlib_bridge_error` (`InvalidDataException`): that is what a GTF and dumps
  from different releases look like.
- **`source_dump` cannot tell species apart.** Ensembl gives every species' dump the same file
  name, so the column holds that one name everywhere, and a caveat says so. `manifest.json`'s
  `inputs` list each dump with its species and sha256.
- **Join with `proteins_resolve_genes()` on the gene set.** Its `gene_set_sha256` column and
  `snap$gene_sets$sha256` are the same value when both were counted against the same GTF. Check
  that before joining a resolution to a snapshot.
- **It is slow and large.** Every input is read whole. For human, mouse and rat at release 116,
  mzLib reports about 20 s to build and 40 s more to write 13 files (9.0 MB).

## What to cite

The methods and resources behind the functions on this page, from their specs:

<!-- BEGIN cite: generated by scripts/render-cite.R from the verb specs; do not edit -->

- [doi:10.1101/gr.073585.107](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.073585.107): Ensembl Compara gene trees, the duplication-aware phylogenies its orthology and paralogy calls are read from (Vilella et al. 2009, Genome Res 19:327).
- [doi:10.1093/nar/gkaf1239](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaf1239): Ensembl releases, their GTFs and the Compara homology dumps (Ensembl 2026, NAR).
- [doi:10.1093/nar/gkae1010](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkae1010): UniProt, whose XML dbReferences carry the gene links resolved (UniProt Consortium 2025, NAR).
- [doi:10.1016/0022-2836(70)90057-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-2836%2870%2990057-4): Global alignment by dynamic programming (Needleman and Wunsch 1970, J Mol Biol 48:443).
- [doi:10.1016/0022-2836(82)90398-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-2836%2882%2990398-9): Affine gap costs in the same time and memory order, the form mzLib implements (Gotoh 1982, J Mol Biol 162:705).
- [doi:10.1073/pnas.89.22.10915](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.89.22.10915): BLOSUM62, the substitution matrix and its half-bit units (Henikoff and Henikoff 1992, PNAS 89:10915).
- [doi:10.1093/genetics/iyad031](https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyad031): The Gene Ontology knowledgebase in 2023 (GO Consortium, Genetics 224, iyad031), the ontology and annotations used.
- [doi:10.1038/75556](https://doi.org/10.1038/75556): Gene Ontology: tool for the unification of biology (Ashburner et al., Nat Genet 25, 25-29, 2000), the is_a / part_of graph propagated over.
- [doi:10.1093/nar/gkv1189](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv1189): RefSeq, whose protein accession prefixes and .n versions mzLib matches (O'Leary et al. 2016, NAR).
